newsitem.title: USA: Stocks hit new high, bonds, oil rally on data, Iraq jitters.
newsitem.headline: Stocks hit new high, bonds, oil rally on data, Iraq jitters.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks surged to a record high while bond rates slid below 7 percent Friday as fresh signs of mild inflation bolstered hopes that the Federal Reserve would not raise interest rates.
The dollar got a boost from the stock and bond rallies.

Oil prices climbed to post-Gulf War highs as world markets braced for U.S. military action against Iraq, but fell after Iraq said it would halt attacks on U.S. and allied warplanes flying over the country.
At around 1:40 p.m. EDT, the Dow Jones industrial average was up 73.98 points, or 1.29 percent, to 5,845.92, smashing the record 5,796.1 intraday high set on May 23.
In the broader market, advancing issues beat declines 17-6 on heavy volume of 321 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index jumped 18.95 points, or 1.63 percent, to 1,184.76 as technology stocks awakened from their recent slumber.
The Labour Department reported that consumer prices rose a mere 0.1 percent in August, helping the inflation-sensitive bond market to sharp gains, which carried over into stocks.
The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond gained 1-21/32, sending its yield below the psychologically key 7 percent level to 6.94 percent from 7.08 percent at Thursday's close.
With the Dow finally able to establish a new high and technology stocks fully participating in the rally, analysts saw signs a new surge could be underway.

"Mood, momentum and money flow are back in gear," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co. "This is the magic moment that people have talked so often about, the Dow has broken through 5,800 and now some have lifted their sights to 6,000."
Technology stocks staged a particularly strong rally, sparked by votes of confidence from several investment firms.
SoundView Financial Group raised its recommended short-term weighting on the sector, saying it expected the group to outperform the broader market.

"We believe that over the next four to five months technology stocks as measured by the SoundView Index should outperform the broader averages on both a relative and absolute basis," SoundView's president and market strategist James Townsend said in a statement.
The dollar rose to 1.5147 marks and 110.43 yen from 1.5130 marks and 110.13 yen late Thursday.
The dollar had inched up to an eight-week high against the German mark Thursday, before gains were eroded by mild U.S. inflation data that tempered prospects of an interest rate increase by the Fed.
On the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil rose as high as $25.35, flirting with the post-Gulf war high of $25.70 a barrel set on April 16.
It was the highest level reached since the 1991 U.S.-led Gulf War, when allied forces launched at attack on Iraq to liberate Kuwait.

October crude fell 30 cents to $24.70 at around 1:30 EDT after the Iraq News Agency, quoting an official spokesman for Iraq's government, said it would halt its attacks on U.S. and allied warplanes flying over its north and south.
World oil prices have risen about $2 a barrel since the U.S.-Iraq tensions started two weeks ago, and are unlikely to correct until the crisis is resolved, oil experts said.
